analysis.title: Dual Mandate Snapshot, October 2026
key_insights: September nonfarm payrolls rose 29k, below expectations, and the unemployment rate ticked up to 4.2%. Job openings also fell. The labor market is cooling but stable and is not adding inflationary pressure.

Wage growth remains subdued. The 3-month annualized rate was 2.7% in September, down from 3.2% in Sep-25. Natixis says this suggests the labor market may be less stable than the headline numbers imply.
Natixis expects the Fed to keep its focus on inflation rather than the labor market.
PCE methodology changes revised the July and August readings down. September inflation was hotter than expected and broad-based, which raised PCE on the year.
Higher energy prices from renewed Middle East tensions drove headline inflation. Energy accounted for more than half of the rise in headline CPI.

The Fed will use the October print to judge whether the September rebound is a one-off or the start of a trend. Natixis thinks the Fed will use the period before its December meeting to plan another hike at that meeting.
Headline CPI rose 0.6% m/m (0.65 in the heat map) and core CPI 0.3% m/m (0.33) in September. Core services rose 0.37% and core goods 0.25%.
Shelter rose 0.41% m/m in September. Rent of primary residence rose 0.25% and owners' equivalent rent 0.35%, both accelerating. The 3-month shelter trend continued to ease.
Energy commodities CPI rose 9.32% m/m in September. Brent averaged $95.69 a barrel and gasoline $4.36 a gallon.

Natixis says labor market indicators point to easing, not rising, labor-driven inflation pressure. Job openings have stabilized and there is about one opening per job seeker, but the low-hire, low-fire pattern persists.
Median unemployment duration rose to 11.45 weeks (3-month average) while continuing claims fell to 1,772k and initial claims to 206k.
Inflation expectations rose in the market-based measures. The 1y swap reached 4.52% and 1y1y 4.91%. 10y breakevens were little changed at 2.35%, and the 5y5y swap was 2.34%.
The 3-month annualized wage measures and AHE y/y (3.02%) continue to decelerate, and real average hourly earnings remain negative.
CBO anticipates net immigration will slow, which Natixis says could signal a wage growth rebound. The report charts a correlation of r=-0.87 between immigration and wages with a 22-month lead.
AI-related job cuts remain at thousands per month, and job gains have declined in sectors most exposed to AI. Implied layoffs in September were below normal levels.
Financial conditions remain loose across Chicago Fed, OFR, Bloomberg, Kansas City Fed and St. Louis Fed measures. The Fed Board growth impulse signals the tailwind is moving closer to neutral.
Policy rules remain slightly above the current fed funds rate. The fed funds target is 3.75%-4.00%.

On the 2026 midterms, Natixis assumes divided government. It expects Democrats to use their leverage to try to roll back healthcare and food assistance cuts from the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill, and notes Democrats' generic ballot lead widened.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Softer than expected. Signals cooling labor demand with no added inflationary pulse.
Ticked up slightly. Labor market is cooling but stable.
Hotter than expected, driven by energy prices. Energy accounted for more than half of the rise.
Broad-based pressure. Core CPI also rose on the year.
Up from 3.35% in August on higher energy prices.
Natixis expects another hike at the December meeting.
Natixis thinks the Fed will use the period before December to plan the hike, after the October inflation print shows whether September was a one-off.
Headline PCE also ticked up. The increase in core was driven by services on the month.
Up from $82.45 in August, feeding energy CPI.

risk_factors: The October inflation print may show the September rebound is the start of a trend, supporting a December hike.
If job openings resume a downward trend, unemployment rate would face upward pressure.
Renewed Middle East tensions could keep energy prices elevated.
A slowdown in net immigration could push wage growth higher.
Subdued wage growth may mean the labor market is less stable than headline numbers imply.
charts_described: Energy accounted for more than half of the rise in headline CPI in September, per the CPI component heat map.
Labor market tightness indicators, shown as z-scores, trend downward, which Natixis reads as easing labor-driven inflation pressure.
geopolitical: Renewed tensions in the Middle East raised energy prices and drove headline inflation in September.
The 2026 midterm elections are expected to produce divided government, with Democrats' leverage over funding and the debt ceiling.

tension_points.bull_case: The labor market is stable. Job openings have stabilized, continuing claims have declined, and there is about one opening per job seeker.
tension_points.bear_case: Payrolls were soft at 29k, unemployment rose to 4.2%, wage growth is subdued and unemployment duration is rising, so the labor market may be less stable than headlines imply.
tension_points.what_invalidates: If job openings resume a downward trend, that would imply upward pressure on the unemployment rate.
